t.1.218.1: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: As he rained down water, the Pāṇḍava Bībhatsu held it back with a shower of arrows, displaying his supreme weapons.
t.1.218.2: And the Pāṇḍava covered the whole Khāṇḍava on every side with his arrows, drawing that rain away from the forest.
t.1.218.4: But Takṣaka, the mighty king of serpents, was not there; while that forest was burning, he was at that time in Kurukṣetra.
t.1.218.3: And no creature whatsoever could escape from there, while the forest was being covered over with arrows by Savyasācin as he kept shooting.
t.1.218.5: But Aśvasena, the mighty son of Takṣaka, was there; he made a fierce effort to free himself from the oblation-bearing fire.
t.1.218.6: Tormented by the arrows of Kaunteya, he was unable to escape; his mother, a serpent's daughter, swallowed him and so set him free.
t.1.218.7: His head had been swallowed first, and his tail was being swallowed, while the she-serpent, anxious for her son, rose upward.
t.1.218.8: With a sharp, broad-edged bhalla arrow the Pāṇḍava cut off her head as she was fleeing, and the lord of the gods saw her.
t.1.218.9: Wishing to set him free, the wielder of the thunderbolt bewildered the Pāṇḍava at that moment with a storm of wind and rain, and so Aśvasena was released.
t.1.218.11: And the enraged Bībhatsu, together with Pāvaka and Vāsudeva, cursed that crooked-moving one, saying, "May you be without a resting place!"
t.1.218.10: Then, seeing that dreadful illusion and deceived by the serpent, he cut those moving through the sky into two and three pieces, O Bhārata.
t.1.218.12: Then Jiṣṇu, enraged and remembering that deception, covered the sky with sharp arrows and fought the thousand-eyed one.
t.1.218.13: The king of the gods too, seeing that Phalguna was as if enraged, released his own blazing weapon, which spread across the entire sky.
t.1.218.14: Then the Wind, with a mighty roar, stirring up all the oceans, stood in the sky and brought forth turbulent clouds pouring down torrents of water.
t.1.218.15: To counter it, Arjuna, skilled in finding the right response, consecrated with mantras and released a supreme weapon, the Vāyavya itself.
t.1.218.17: And in a moment the sky became one in which dust and darkness had wholly subsided, with the pleasant quality of a cool breeze, and with the sun's disk restored to its natural state.
t.1.218.16: By that, the might and force of Indra's thunderbolts and clouds was destroyed; those torrents of water dried up, and the lightning flashes vanished.
t.1.218.18: And the oblation-eater, delighted at meeting no resistance, assuming manifold forms and possessed of matchless flames, blazed up, filling the world with his roars.
t.1.218.20: Garuḍas too, eager to strike Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava with their wings, beaks and talons hard as the thunderbolt, swooped down from the sky.
t.1.218.21: Likewise, hosts of serpents with blazing mouths, spewing dreadful venom, sallied forth close to the Pāṇḍava.
t.1.218.19: Seeing that burning forest guarded by the two Kṛṣṇas, the proud birds, Suparṇa and the others, then flew up together into the sky.
t.1.218.23: Then the gods, together with the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas and Pannagas, eager for battle, rose up, letting out an unequalled roar.
t.1.218.22: Seeing the sky-ranging creatures enraged, Pārtha cut them down with his arrows, and, helpless, they fell into the blazing fire, to the destruction of their bodies.
t.1.218.24: With arms upraised bearing iron darts, discuses, stones and bhuśuṇḍis, their might swelled by wrath, they sought to slay Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha.
t.1.218.25: As they shouted out and loosed a rain of weapons, Bībhatsu crushed their heads with his sharpened arrows.
t.1.218.26: And Kṛṣṇa too, of exceedingly great splendor, slayer of foes with his discus, then wrought a great slaughter among the hosts of Daityas and Dānavas.
t.1.218.27: Then others of great might, pierced by arrows and driven by the force of the discus, came to a halt, like the sea that has reached its shore.
t.1.218.28: Then Śakra, the great lord of the thirty gods, filled with fury, mounted his white elephant and charged at the two of them.
t.1.218.29: Swiftly seizing the thunderbolt, the slayer of the Asuras hurled the Vajra weapon and said to the gods, “These two are slain.”
t.1.218.30: Then, seeing the great thunderbolt raised aloft by the lord of the gods, the gods at that moment seized all their weapons, each his own.
t.1.218.32: The two Aśvins too took up blazing herbs; Dhātṛ seized a bow, and Jaya likewise a club.
t.1.218.33: And the mighty Tvaṣṭā, enraged, seized a mountain; Aṃśa took up a spear, and the god Mṛtyu an axe.
t.1.218.31: King Yama took up the staff of Time, the Lord of Riches his litter, Varuṇa there his noose, and Śiva likewise the vicakra.
t.1.218.34: Aryaman too, grasping a terrible iron club, moved about, and Mitra, taking up a discus edged with razors, stood ready.
t.1.218.37: These and many other gods, bearing various weapons and seeking to slay those two best of men, Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha, advanced against them.
t.1.218.35: Pūṣan and the enraged Bhaga and Savitṛ, O lord of the people, took up their bows and swords and rushed upon Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha.
t.1.218.38: There, in that great battle, wondrous portents were seen, O Bhārata, resembling those at the end of a yuga, foreboding the destruction of living beings.
t.1.218.39: But seeing Śakra thus enraged, together with the gods, the two unshaken ones, fearless and invincible in battle, stood firm with their bows strung and ready.
t.1.218.40: Then, seeing those gods arrive one by one, the two, enraged, held them back with arrows like thunderbolts.
t.1.218.41: Again and again the gods were made to have their resolve broken, many times over; abandoning the battle out of fear, they sought refuge with Śakra alone.
t.1.218.36: The Rudras and the Vasus, and the mighty Maruts, the Viśvedevas and likewise the Sādhyas, blazing with their own splendor, came forth.
t.1.218.42: Seeing the gods held back by Mādhava and Arjuna, the sages stationed there in the sky were filled with wonder.
t.1.218.43: And Śakra too, having repeatedly witnessed the valor of those two in battle, became supremely pleased, and he made them fight once more.
t.1.218.44: Then Pākaśāsana released a very great shower of stones, wishing once more to test the valour of Savyasācin. Arjuna, utterly intolerant of it, struck back that shower with his arrows.
t.1.218.45: And Śatakratu, seeing that rain being rendered fruitless, then, as king of the gods, made that rain increase once more.
t.1.218.47: Then, tearing off with both hands a great peak from Mandara, together with its trees, Śakra hurled it, seeking to slay the son of Pāṇḍu.
t.1.218.46: Then the son of Pākaśāsana, with arrows of great speed, brought that shower of stones to destruction, delighting his father.
t.1.218.48: Then Arjuna, with swift, straight-flying arrows whose tips were blazing, shattered the mountain's peak into a thousand pieces.
t.1.218.49: The appearance of that mountain as it was shattering then shone like that of the sky with its sun, moon and planets breaking apart.
t.1.218.50: By that great mountain falling headlong into the burning forest, the creatures dwelling in Khāṇḍava were slain there in even greater numbers.
